en.title: The Indus Valley Civilization
en.place: Indus Valley, present-day Pakistan and northwestern India
en.text:
## A civilization of planned cities

The Indus Valley Civilization, also called the Harappan Civilization, was one of the earliest urban societies of the ancient world. Its mature urban phase flourished roughly between 2600 and 1900 BCE, across a vast region covering much of present-day Pakistan and northwestern India. Its settlements extended from the highlands and foothills to the Indus river system and the plains of Gujarat. The civilization is named after Harappa, one of the first major sites excavated, while Mohenjo-daro became its best-known urban centre.

The scale of this society is striking. Archaeologists have identified hundreds of settlements, ranging from large cities to towns, villages and specialised production sites. The two famous cities, Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, reveal carefully planned streets, brick buildings, wells, drains and public structures. Their urban design suggests that civic organisation and shared standards were important across a wide territory.

## Cities, water and everyday life

Many Indus buildings used standardised fired bricks, often made in consistent proportions. Streets commonly followed planned alignments, while houses were arranged around courtyards. Some homes had bathing areas connected to drains. Covered drainage channels, inspection points and numerous wells demonstrate sustained attention to water management and sanitation. The so-called Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro was a carefully constructed tank whose precise purpose remains debated; it may have served ritual or communal functions.

These features should not be mistaken for proof of a single central government controlling every city. Similar building standards may have emerged through shared traditions, commercial networks, political coordination or a combination of institutions. The evidence does show that people could organise labour, manufacture standard materials and maintain complex urban infrastructure.

Most inhabitants probably worked in agriculture, animal husbandry, crafts and trade. Wheat and barley were important crops in many areas, while evidence also points to pulses, sesame, dates and regionally varied cultivation. Cattle, sheep, goats and water buffalo were among the animals kept. Cotton was used for textiles, making the Indus region one of the earliest known centres of cotton production.

## Crafts and long-distance exchange

Indus artisans produced pottery, beads, ornaments, metal objects, shell goods and finely worked stone. Carnelian beads, sometimes treated through heating and drilling techniques, demonstrate specialised knowledge. Seals carved with animals and short inscriptions are among the most recognisable objects associated with the civilization. They may have been used to identify people, goods, institutions or commercial transactions, although their exact functions are not fully understood.

Trade connected Indus communities with regions beyond the subcontinent. Archaeological evidence and Mesopotamian texts refer to a land called Meluhha, widely associated by scholars with the Indus region. Indus materials and seals have been found in Gulf and Mesopotamian contexts, while imported raw materials reached Indus settlements. Copper, precious stones, shell and other resources moved through networks linking coastal communities, inland towns and distant markets.

The civilization therefore belonged to a wider Bronze Age world in which cities and states exchanged commodities, technologies and ideas. Its merchants and craftspeople were not isolated; they participated in networks extending across the Arabian Sea and the Persian Gulf.

## Writing and unresolved questions

The Indus script appears on seals, pottery, tablets and other objects. Most inscriptions are short, and the script has not been securely deciphered. Scholars disagree about the language or languages represented and even about some aspects of how the signs functioned. Without a readable archive, historians must rely heavily on archaeology, environmental evidence and comparisons with neighbouring societies.

This limitation matters. It is not possible to reconstruct named rulers, dynasties or detailed political events with confidence. No universally accepted royal palace or monumental tomb has been identified at the major cities. The material record suggests social complexity, but it does not reveal the exact form of authority or the beliefs of all communities.

## Transformation and legacy

After about 1900 BCE, many large urban centres declined or were abandoned. This was not necessarily a sudden collapse of the entire population. Settlement patterns shifted, long-distance exchange changed and communities increasingly occupied smaller towns and rural sites. Changes in river systems, weakening monsoon patterns, floods, droughts and economic reorganisation have all been investigated as possible contributing factors. Current research generally treats the transformation as complex and regionally varied rather than the result of one catastrophe.

The Indus tradition did not simply disappear. People continued to live across the region, adapting settlement, farming and craft practices. Some cultural continuities may have contributed to later South Asian traditions, although direct links are difficult to establish in the absence of deciphered texts.

The Indus Valley Civilization is important because it demonstrates an early and distinctive path to urban life. Its cities were not replicas of Mesopotamia or Egypt. Their planning, water systems, craft production and commercial reach show how communities in South Asia developed sophisticated institutions and technologies on their own historical terms.

en.title: The Achaemenid Persian Empire
en.place: Western and Central Asia, from the Iranian plateau
en.text:
## The rise of an imperial power

The Achaemenid Persian Empire was one of the largest political formations of the ancient world. It emerged in the sixth century BCE under Cyrus II, commonly known as Cyrus the Great, and developed into an empire stretching from parts of the Balkans and Egypt to Central Asia and the Indus region. Its rulers governed an extraordinary diversity of languages, religions, landscapes and political traditions.

Before Cyrus, the Persians were one of several Iranian-speaking peoples living on the Iranian plateau. Cyrus, a ruler of Anshan in southwestern Iran, defeated the Median king Astyages around 550 BCE and brought a wider territory under his control. He then conquered Lydia in Anatolia and captured Babylon in 539 BCE. These victories created the foundation of an empire whose power rested on military strength, diplomacy, taxation and the cooperation of local elites.

## Cyrus and imperial government

Cyrus is remembered in different ways by different historical traditions. Greek authors presented him as a remarkable founder, while Babylonian records describe his entry into Babylon and his adoption of established royal titles. The object known as the Cyrus Cylinder records his presentation of himself as a restorer of temples and proper order. It is a valuable example of royal ideology, but it should not be read as a modern declaration of universal human rights.

The Achaemenid rulers generally allowed local religious institutions and customs to continue when these did not threaten imperial authority. Such flexibility helped them govern territories with long-established political and cultural systems. Local officials, aristocrats, priests and scribes remained important, even as imperial administrators supervised taxation, communications and security.

Darius I, who ruled from 522 to 486 BCE, strengthened the administrative structure. The empire was divided into provinces often called satrapies, each governed by a satrap. The system was not identical everywhere and changed over time. Royal inspectors, military commanders and other officials helped prevent provincial governors from becoming entirely independent.

## Roads, communication and resources

The empire's Royal Road system and other routes connected important centres. The famous road between Susa and Sardis helped officials, couriers, merchants and armies travel across long distances. Relay stations and organised messengers improved the movement of information. These networks were essential to the management of a territory too large for a ruler to supervise personally.

Imperial revenue came from taxes, tribute, agricultural production, trade and access to valuable resources. Darius introduced a standard gold coin, the daric, alongside silver coinage, although many local currencies and systems of exchange continued. The empire also used labour obligations and organised workforces for royal construction projects.

Persepolis, founded under Darius and expanded by his successors, became a major ceremonial centre. Its terraces, palaces and reliefs depict delegations bringing gifts from across the empire. The images communicate a vision of ordered diversity: different peoples are represented in distinctive clothing, participating in a hierarchy centred on the Great King.

## Religion and royal ideology

Achaemenid inscriptions frequently invoke Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity in the royal religious language. Darius presented legitimate kingship as supported by Ahura Mazda and described rebellion as a form of disorder or falsehood. The relationship between Achaemenid royal practice and the later development of Zoroastrianism remains a subject of scholarly discussion. It is clear that religious life across the empire was diverse, and that local cults continued in many regions.

Royal ideology linked the king with justice, order and the protection of the realm. Monumental inscriptions, palace reliefs and ceremonial architecture made this message visible. The king's authority was personal and dynastic, but it depended on a broad network of administrators, soldiers and local collaborators.

## Conflict with Greece and imperial limits

The Achaemenids fought a series of conflicts with Greek city-states. The Ionian Revolt began in 499 BCE, and the Persian campaigns against mainland Greece included the battles of Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis and Plataea. Greek accounts, especially those of Herodotus, shaped later memories of these wars. They must be read critically because they reflect particular Greek perspectives and literary aims.

The empire remained powerful for generations after the wars. Its rulers campaigned in Egypt, Anatolia and Central Asia, while managing revolts and dynastic disputes. In the fourth century BCE, internal instability and regional resistance weakened imperial control. Alexander of Macedon invaded in 334 BCE, defeated Darius III and captured the principal royal centres. By 330 BCE, Achaemenid imperial rule had ended.

## Historical significance

The Achaemenid Empire influenced later political traditions across the Middle East and beyond. Its provincial administration, road networks, royal ideology and methods of integrating local elites offered models that successor states adapted. Alexander retained many administrative practices, and later Iranian empires developed their own forms of large-scale kingship.

The empire should not be understood as a uniform state imposed on passive populations. It was a negotiated political system that combined conquest with accommodation. Its history reveals how a vast empire could maintain authority across cultural boundaries while remaining dependent on local institutions and regional conditions.

en.title: The Maurya Empire
en.place: South Asia, centred on the Gangetic plain
en.text:
## Unification after the age of the mahajanapadas

The Maurya Empire was the first South Asian empire to unite much of the subcontinent under one ruling dynasty. It emerged around 322 BCE, after the political competition of the mahajanapadas and the expansion of Magadha in the Gangetic plain. Its founder, Chandragupta Maurya, established a powerful state with its centre at Pataliputra, near modern Patna in Bihar.

The circumstances of Chandragupta's rise are known through a mixture of later Indian traditions, Greek accounts and archaeological evidence. Classical writers describe a ruler called Sandrokottos, generally identified with Chandragupta, who came to power after Alexander's campaigns in the northwest. Chandragupta's state expanded across northern India and entered into conflict and diplomacy with Seleucus I, one of Alexander's successors. A treaty around 305 BCE established a political settlement and involved the exchange of territories and diplomatic relations.

## Administration and imperial reach

The Maurya state governed a large and diverse territory. Pataliputra served as a major political centre, while provincial centres helped administer distant regions. The empire relied on officials responsible for revenue, justice, roads, security and local administration. The exact structure is debated because some famous descriptions, especially the Arthashastra, are complex texts whose date and relationship to Mauryan practice remain contested.

Agriculture provided the principal economic foundation. The fertile plains of northern India supported dense populations and substantial tax revenues. Irrigation, land clearance, craft production and trade contributed to the wealth of the state. Roads linked cities, market towns and frontier regions, while merchants moved textiles, metals, agricultural products and luxury goods.

The Mauryas also maintained a significant military establishment. Greek sources describe infantry, cavalry, chariots and elephants, although the details may reflect external observation and later reporting. The army helped secure territory, but the empire's survival also depended on alliances, local officials and negotiated relationships with communities beyond the core.

## Ashoka and the Kalinga war

The most famous Mauryan ruler was Ashoka, who came to the throne in the third century BCE, commonly dated to about 268 BCE. Early in his reign he fought a major campaign against Kalinga, a region on the eastern coast of the subcontinent. In his own inscriptions, Ashoka describes the suffering caused by the conquest and expresses deep remorse for the deaths, deportations and disruption that followed.

Ashoka's response was expressed through the policy he called dhamma. This was an ethical programme emphasising respect for parents and teachers, humane treatment of servants, restraint, generosity, religious tolerance and concern for living beings. Dhamma was not simply identical with Buddhist doctrine, even though Ashoka became a major patron of Buddhism. His inscriptions address a broad population and promote conduct that could support social harmony across religious and cultural differences.

## Inscriptions and communication

Ashoka's inscriptions are among the most important primary sources for ancient South Asian history. They were placed on rocks and pillars in different parts of the empire. Most were written in Prakrit using scripts such as Brahmi and Kharosthi, while some frontier inscriptions used Greek and Aramaic. Their languages and scripts show that imperial communication adapted to regional audiences.

The inscriptions describe royal instructions, ethical concerns, administrative measures and the appointment of officials known as dhamma-mahamattas. They also record Ashoka's interest in medical provision, roads, wells and the welfare of humans and animals. These statements reveal the ideals the king wished to publicise; they do not prove that every policy was implemented equally in every province.

Ashoka's support helped Buddhism gain visibility and institutional strength. Buddhist traditions later remembered missions sent to other regions, including Sri Lanka. The details of these missions are preserved in religious chronicles and must be assessed alongside other evidence. Ashoka's inscriptions nevertheless demonstrate a ruler deliberately using public writing to communicate moral and political messages across a vast territory.

## Decline and legacy

After Ashoka's death, the empire gradually weakened. The causes are uncertain and probably included succession disputes, the difficulty of maintaining distant provinces, regional political change and pressures on imperial resources. The last Maurya ruler, Brihadratha, was overthrown around 185 BCE by Pushyamitra Shunga, according to later historical accounts.

The Maurya Empire left a lasting mark on South Asian political memory. Ashoka's pillars and inscriptions became central to modern historical understanding, and the lion capital from Sarnath was adopted as the emblem of the Republic of India. The wheel associated with Ashoka appears at the centre of India's national flag.

The empire's significance lies not only in territorial expansion. It offers an unusually rich view of ancient statecraft, imperial communication and the relationship between power and ethical ideals. Ashoka's attempt to define a moral language for government remains one of the most distinctive experiments in the political history of the ancient world.

en.title: The Gupta Empire
en.text:
## The emergence of Gupta power

The Gupta Empire became one of the most influential political and cultural powers in northern South Asia between the fourth and sixth centuries CE. Its rulers governed a changing network of territories centred on the Gangetic plain, and their period is often associated with major achievements in Sanskrit literature, mathematics, astronomy, sculpture and religious thought. The label “Golden Age” is sometimes used, but it can obscure regional diversity, social inequality and the fact that cultural production continued beyond the Gupta court.

The dynasty's early history is not fully clear. Chandragupta I, who ruled in the early fourth century, strengthened the family's position through alliances and territorial expansion. His son Samudragupta conducted campaigns across northern India and established influence over rulers in other regions. His achievements are recorded in the Allahabad pillar inscription, composed by the court poet Harishena. The inscription praises the king's victories and presents an ideal of universal sovereignty, so it must be read as royal eulogy as well as historical evidence.

## Political organisation and diplomacy

Gupta rule did not always mean direct administration. The empire included core territories under closer royal control, subordinate rulers who acknowledged Gupta authority, and regions connected through alliances, tribute or military relationships. This flexible arrangement allowed the dynasty to project power across a large area without maintaining the same administrative presence everywhere.

Land grants became increasingly important in political and economic life. Rulers granted land or revenue rights to religious institutions and individuals, often recording these grants on copper plates or stone inscriptions. Such grants could strengthen royal alliances and support religious communities, but they also transferred resources and authority to local beneficiaries. Over time, these arrangements contributed to the growth of regional power centres.

The Guptas issued gold coins depicting rulers in different roles, including military, ritual and cultural settings. Coinage offers evidence for royal image-making, economic resources and political claims. It also demonstrates the importance of gold and long-distance exchange, although coin circulation varied by region and period.

## Learning, literature and science

Sanskrit became a major language of courtly expression and intellectual exchange. The poet and dramatist Kalidasa is traditionally associated with the Gupta age, although the precise dating of his life is uncertain. Works such as Abhijnanashakuntalam and the Meghaduta became enduring classics of Sanskrit literature. Court patronage supported scholars, religious teachers and artists, but learning also took place in monasteries, temples and other institutions.

The mathematician and astronomer Aryabhata, born in 476 CE, wrote the Aryabhatiya, a concise work addressing arithmetic, algebra, geometry, astronomical calculation and the causes of eclipses. He described the rotation of the Earth on its axis and developed methods for calculating planetary positions. The history of the decimal place-value system and the use of zero developed over a long period, involving contributions from multiple scholars and regions; it should not be attributed to one ruler or one moment.

Gupta-period sculpture and architecture also show remarkable technical and aesthetic achievement. Images of Hindu deities developed influential forms, while Buddhist and Jain institutions continued to commission art. Temples increasingly became important centres of worship and patronage. Surviving structures, inscriptions and sculptures reveal interactions between local traditions and broader religious networks.

## Religion and society

The Gupta rulers were often patrons of Hindu traditions, especially forms of Vaishnavism, but their empire contained diverse religious communities. Buddhism and Jainism remained influential, and religious institutions interacted through debate, patronage, pilgrimage and shared urban environments. Royal inscriptions and coins show that rulers used religious symbols to express legitimacy, while local communities maintained their own practices.

Society was structured by hierarchies of status, occupation, gender and caste. Sanskrit legal and religious texts provide ideals and prescriptions, not straightforward descriptions of everyday life. Inscriptions and material evidence show a more varied landscape in which merchants, artisans, farmers, monks, landholders and local chiefs shaped economic and social relations.

## Decline and historical assessment

The empire weakened during the fifth and sixth centuries. Invasions by groups known in Indian sources as the Hunas, conflicts among regional powers, succession problems and the growing autonomy of subordinate rulers all contributed to the decline. Gupta authority fragmented, and new kingdoms emerged across northern India.

The Gupta period remains important because of its cultural and intellectual legacy, not because every part of South Asia experienced uniform prosperity. Its achievements in literature, mathematics, astronomy, art and political expression influenced later centuries. A balanced account recognises both the extraordinary creativity of the period and the unequal social structures within which that creativity flourished.

en.title: The Khmer Empire of Angkor
en.place: Mainland Southeast Asia, centred on Cambodia
en.text:
## The formation of an Angkorian state

The Khmer Empire, often called the Angkorian Empire, dominated much of mainland Southeast Asia from the ninth to the fifteenth centuries. Its political and ceremonial centre was in present-day Cambodia, where the remains of Angkor form one of the world's most remarkable archaeological landscapes. The empire's influence extended at different times into areas now belonging to Thailand, Laos and Vietnam.

A conventional starting point is 802 CE, when Jayavarman II was consecrated as a universal monarch in a ceremony later associated with the formation of a new Khmer kingship. The details come from inscriptions written generations after the event, so the date is a useful historical marker rather than a complete account of a single founding moment. Earlier Khmer-speaking polities and networks already existed in the region.

## Angkor and the management of water

Angkor grew into a vast urban and ceremonial complex. Its temples, reservoirs, canals, roads and settlements were connected to an agricultural landscape that supported a large population. The enormous reservoirs known as baray and the canal systems are often described as a sophisticated hydraulic network. Scholars continue to debate how these systems functioned, how consistently they were maintained and how much they contributed directly to rice production.

Water management was nevertheless central to life in the region. Seasonal monsoon rains alternated with drier periods, and communities developed ways to store, distribute and manage water. Reservoirs could serve practical, symbolic and ritual purposes. The relationship between infrastructure, agriculture and royal authority was complex: large public works demonstrated the ruler's ability to mobilise labour and connect the kingdom through monumental projects.

## Temples, kingship and religion

Angkor's temples are not simply religious buildings; they also express political ideas. Rulers commissioned temples and inscriptions that linked kingship with Hindu and Buddhist cosmologies. Early Angkorian rulers often favoured forms of Hindu worship, including devotion to Shiva and Vishnu. Later rulers supported Mahayana Buddhism, and Theravada Buddhism eventually became dominant in Cambodia.

Angkor Wat, constructed in the first half of the twelfth century under Suryavarman II, is among the most famous monuments. Originally dedicated to Vishnu, it combines a vast temple complex with elaborate bas-reliefs depicting Hindu narratives, royal processions and scenes of battle. The monument's scale and orientation express religious and political meaning, while its artistic programme reflects the skills of specialised builders and sculptors.

Jayavarman VII, who ruled in the late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries, sponsored major construction projects and supported Mahayana Buddhism. The Bayon, with its towers bearing large carved faces, is associated with his reign. He also promoted roads, rest houses and hospitals according to inscriptions, suggesting an ambitious programme of royal infrastructure and welfare.

## Economy and regional connections

The Angkorian economy rested on rice cultivation, fishing, forest resources, craft production and exchange. The Tonle Sap lake and its seasonal flood cycle provided rich fisheries and supported surrounding communities. Inland routes connected agricultural centres with the coast and neighbouring polities, while maritime trade linked Southeast Asia to China, India and the wider Indian Ocean.

The Khmer world was never isolated. Religious ideas, scripts, artistic forms and political concepts circulated through networks connecting South and Southeast Asia. Khmer rulers adapted these influences to local circumstances rather than simply copying foreign models. Sanskrit and Old Khmer inscriptions record land grants, temple foundations, royal genealogies and administrative arrangements.

## Transformation and legacy

From the thirteenth century, the political and economic landscape changed. Theravada Buddhism spread more widely, regional trade patterns shifted and rival powers, including Ayutthaya, challenged Khmer authority. Environmental change, infrastructure maintenance and demographic pressures have also been studied as possible factors in Angkor's transformation. The old capital did not vanish overnight; settlement and political life continued in the region, while the centre of power shifted.

Angkor remains a major source for understanding state formation, religion, urban planning and environmental adaptation in Southeast Asia. Its monuments demonstrate the resources that rulers could mobilise, but they also preserve the work of countless farmers, builders, artisans and communities whose lives made the capital possible.

en.title: The Srivijaya Maritime Empire
en.place: Sumatra and the Strait of Malacca, maritime Southeast Asia
en.text:
## A power built around the sea

Srivijaya was a maritime political and commercial network centred on Sumatra that became influential from around the seventh century CE. Rather than resembling a compact territorial empire with fixed borders, Srivijaya's power depended on ports, river systems, shipping routes, alliances and the ability to influence trade through the Strait of Malacca and nearby waters. Its history is reconstructed from inscriptions, Chinese records, archaeological discoveries and later regional traditions.

One of the earliest important records is the Kedukan Bukit inscription, dated 683 CE, which refers to a ruler named Dapunta Hyang and a successful expedition. Other inscriptions from the Palembang region describe royal authority, religious merit and political organisation. These sources suggest that a centre in southeastern Sumatra became powerful by connecting inland resources with maritime commerce.

## Trade and strategic geography

The Strait of Malacca links the Indian Ocean with the South China Sea. For centuries, ships travelling between western Asia, India, Southeast Asia and China used routes through this region. Monsoon winds shaped sailing schedules, while safe harbours, supplies, pilots and commercial contacts made particular ports valuable.

Srivijaya's rulers benefited from this geography. They could facilitate trade, provide services to merchants, collect duties and build relationships with visiting communities. The polity's influence likely depended on cooperation with local chiefs and port authorities as much as on direct military control. Control of river mouths and coastal passages helped connect forest products, gold and other commodities from the interior with international markets.

Chinese sources describe diplomatic contacts between Srivijaya and the Tang court. These missions were political as well as commercial: rulers sought recognition, access to prestige goods and favourable conditions for exchange. Indian Ocean networks also brought religious teachers, monks and scholars to the region.

## Buddhism and international learning

Srivijaya became known as an important centre of Buddhist learning. The Chinese monk Yijing visited in the seventh century while travelling to and from India. He praised the Buddhist study available in the region and recommended that Chinese monks spend time there before continuing to the great centres of learning in India. His account provides unusually direct evidence for the intellectual connections of maritime Southeast Asia.

Buddhism in Srivijaya was connected to wider networks of monasteries, pilgrimage and textual study. Sanskrit inscriptions and religious objects show the influence of Indian traditions, but local communities shaped their own practices. The movement of monks and manuscripts across the Bay of Bengal illustrates how the sea served as a corridor for ideas as well as goods.

## Political structure and regional relations

The term “Srivijaya” may refer at different times to a ruling centre, a royal title or a wider network of dependent and allied ports. This makes it difficult to draw a precise map of the polity. Its influence shifted as rulers formed alliances, competed with neighbouring powers and responded to changing trade routes.

Srivijaya interacted with Java, the Malay Peninsula, southern Thailand and other coastal societies. The Sailendra dynasty, associated with major Buddhist monuments in Java, has been linked to Srivijaya in some historical interpretations, although the exact political relationship remains debated. The region's history was shaped by overlapping dynasties and maritime networks rather than by a single stable imperial boundary.

## Decline and historical importance

From the eleventh century, Srivijaya faced pressure from rival commercial and political powers. A Chola naval expedition from southern India attacked ports associated with Srivijaya in 1025. The campaign demonstrated the reach of Indian Ocean naval power and disrupted parts of the network, although it did not necessarily destroy Srivijaya immediately. Later changes in trade, regional politics and the rise of other ports further reduced its influence.

Srivijaya's history challenges the idea that major states must be based on extensive inland territory. Its power came from mobility, commercial knowledge and the strategic management of connections. It was also a centre of religious and intellectual exchange, linking South Asia, China and the islands of Southeast Asia. The maritime world it helped shape continued to evolve long after its political prominence faded.

en.title: The Mongol Empire
en.text:
## From steppe confederation to world empire

The Mongol Empire emerged in the early thirteenth century under Temujin, who was proclaimed Chinggis Khan in 1206. From a base in the Mongolian steppe, he united or subordinated rival groups and built a military and political system capable of conquering territories across Eurasia. At its greatest extent, the Mongol imperial world connected East Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East and parts of Eastern Europe.

The steppe environment shaped Mongol society. Pastoral communities relied on herds, seasonal movement and networks of exchange. Political leadership depended on personal loyalty, military skill, alliance-making and the distribution of wealth. Temujin's achievement was not simply to win battles; he reorganised relationships among clans and commanders, creating a broader political identity and a disciplined military structure.

## Conquest and military organisation

Mongol armies were highly mobile and made extensive use of mounted archery, coordinated manoeuvres and intelligence. Their forces could move rapidly across open terrain, divide into units and regroup for major operations. They also adapted siege technology and employed engineers and specialists from conquered territories. The Mongols were not invincible, and their campaigns could be slowed by geography, fortified cities, disease and resistance, but their ability to combine mobility with technical expertise was formidable.

After the conquest of northern China and campaigns in Central Asia, Mongol forces moved west. The invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire in the 1210s and 1220s devastated major cities and transformed the political map of the region. Later campaigns reached the Caucasus, Rus' principalities, Persia and the Middle East. Under Chinggis Khan's successors, Mongol armies also conquered much of China and established rule over large areas of Eurasia.

## Governance and communication

Mongol rule varied considerably from region to region. The empire used local administrators, tax officials, scribes and religious authorities, while Mongol princes and military elites retained ultimate political power. In some territories, existing institutions continued under new supervision; elsewhere, conquest brought severe destruction and demographic disruption.

A system of relay stations and supply points, often called the yam, helped officials and messengers travel across long distances. The empire issued travel permissions and protected selected merchants and envoys. These measures facilitated communication and exchange, although safety and prosperity were uneven and could be interrupted by conflict or political division.

The Mongols were generally pragmatic in religious matters. Their empire included Muslims, Christians, Buddhists, Daoists, Jews and followers of other traditions. Rulers employed religious specialists and sometimes granted privileges to institutions whose support was useful. This pluralism did not mean that all communities enjoyed equal treatment, but it enabled the empire to govern a diverse population.

## The empire divides

After Chinggis Khan's death in 1227, his descendants expanded the empire and divided authority among branches of the ruling family. Over time, several major khanates emerged: the Yuan dynasty in China under Kublai Khan, the Ilkhanate in Persia, the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia and the Golden Horde in the western steppe. These states maintained connections but increasingly pursued their own political interests.

Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and completed the conquest of the Southern Song in 1279. Mongol rule in China adopted many Chinese administrative practices while retaining a hierarchy that privileged Mongols and certain allied groups. In Persia, the Ilkhans gradually adopted Islam, while the Golden Horde developed close ties with Muslim societies.

## Exchange, violence and legacy

The Mongol period intensified connections across Eurasia. Merchants, diplomats, religious figures, artisans and technologies moved along routes that later historians associate with the Pax Mongolica. This phrase should not suggest universal peace: warfare, taxation, forced migration and epidemics remained part of imperial life. The movement of people and goods also contributed to the spread of diseases, including the conditions that enabled the Black Death to travel across Eurasia in the fourteenth century.

The Mongol Empire transformed political boundaries and linked regions that had previously interacted less directly. Its legacy includes new states, altered trade networks, military innovations and enduring memories of conquest. A balanced history must hold together both sides of this record: the extraordinary connectivity created by Mongol rule and the immense human cost of its expansion.

en.title: The Ottoman Empire
en.place: Anatolia, southeastern Europe, North Africa and the Middle East
en.text:
## A frontier principality becomes an empire

The Ottoman Empire began as a small principality in northwestern Anatolia around the end of the thirteenth century. Its early rulers expanded into territories held by Byzantine and other regional powers. The dynasty takes its name from Osman I, whose leadership and descendants built a state that eventually governed parts of southeastern Europe, western Asia and North Africa for more than six centuries.

The early Ottoman polity grew in a frontier environment where political authority was fragmented and military opportunity was frequent. Its rulers attracted warriors, administrators and settlers, while making alliances with neighbouring powers. Expansion was not a simple or uninterrupted process; it depended on diplomacy, warfare, dynastic succession and the ability to incorporate local elites.

## Constantinople and imperial transformation

A decisive turning point came in 1453, when Sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople after a major siege. The city, formerly the capital of the Byzantine Empire, became the Ottoman imperial centre and was later known as Istanbul. Its strategic position connected the Black Sea, the Mediterranean and routes between Europe and Asia. Mehmed II rebuilt and repopulated the city, making it a centre of government, commerce and religious life.

Under Selim I and Suleiman I in the sixteenth century, Ottoman power expanded dramatically. The empire incorporated Syria, Egypt and the holy cities of Mecca and Medina after defeating the Mamluk Sultanate in 1516–1517. Ottoman fleets and armies competed across the Mediterranean, Red Sea and Persian Gulf. Suleiman's reign became associated with imperial wealth, legal development, architecture and military power.

## Government and society

The Ottoman state combined dynastic authority with a sophisticated administrative structure. The sultan stood at the centre of government, supported by the imperial council, senior officials, provincial governors and military institutions. The devshirme system recruited some Christian boys from the empire's Balkan provinces for training in state service and the Janissary corps. The system created powerful servants of the state but also involved coercive practices and cannot be separated from the unequal conditions of imperial rule.

The empire's population was religiously and linguistically diverse. Muslim communities formed the political core, while Orthodox Christians, Armenians, Jews and other groups maintained religious institutions and communal structures. The arrangements often described as the millet system evolved over time and varied by place; they should not be imagined as a single fixed constitutional framework. Local communities paid taxes, negotiated privileges and interacted with imperial officials in different ways.

Ottoman law combined dynastic regulations with Islamic jurisprudence. Courts, judges and legal scholars played important roles in daily life, while local customs continued to shape property, family and commercial practices. The empire's cities were centres of craft production, trade, learning and religious patronage.

## Economy, architecture and culture

Ottoman economic life connected agricultural regions, urban workshops and long-distance trade. Istanbul, Cairo, Aleppo, Bursa, Salonica and other cities served as important commercial centres. The state sought revenue through land taxation, customs duties and control of strategic routes. Its economic fortunes changed with warfare, demographic shifts, inflation, maritime competition and the changing patterns of global trade.

Ottoman architecture remains one of the most visible expressions of imperial culture. Sinan, the celebrated sixteenth-century architect, designed mosques and public complexes that combined engineering, religious symbolism and urban planning. The Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul is a major example. Ottoman calligraphy, ceramics, textiles, music and manuscript arts also developed distinctive styles while drawing on a wide range of regional influences.

## Reform, nationalism and dissolution

From the eighteenth century, Ottoman rulers faced military competition from European powers, fiscal pressures and growing challenges from within the empire. Reform efforts sought to reorganise the army, administration, education and taxation. The Tanzimat reforms of the nineteenth century aimed to strengthen the state and redefine relations between subjects and government, but their implementation was uneven.

Nationalist movements, wars, foreign intervention and internal political conflict weakened imperial authority. The Young Turk movement and the constitutional changes of 1908 reshaped politics, while the First World War brought catastrophic losses. The empire's wartime leadership became associated with mass violence, including the Armenian Genocide, as well as the displacement and suffering of many other communities.

After defeat in the First World War, the sultanate was abolished in 1922 and the Republic of Turkey was proclaimed in 1923 under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk. Other former Ottoman territories came under mandates or new political arrangements.

## Historical significance

The Ottoman Empire shaped the histories of the Balkans, Middle East, North Africa and eastern Mediterranean. Its institutions, legal traditions, architecture, foodways and languages left deep legacies. Its history cannot be reduced either to a story of decline or to imperial splendour: it was a changing, multi-ethnic state whose power depended on negotiation, adaptation and coercion over many centuries.

en.title: The Inca Empire
en.place: Andean South America, centred on Cusco
en.text:
## The rise of Tawantinsuyu

The Inca Empire, known in Quechua as Tawantinsuyu, was the largest state in pre-Columbian South America. It developed around Cusco in the Andes and expanded rapidly during the fifteenth century. At its height, it extended along much of the western side of the continent, covering territories in present-day Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Chile, Argentina and Colombia.

Inca traditions remembered a long line of rulers, but the empire's rapid expansion is especially associated with Pachacuti, who ruled in the fifteenth century. After defeating rival powers around Cusco, he reorganised the state and began a programme of conquest and construction. His successors, including Topa Inca Yupanqui and Huayna Capac, extended imperial authority across a vast and geographically varied region.

## Roads and administration

The Andes presented extraordinary challenges to imperial government. Mountains, deserts, high plateaus and deep valleys separated communities and made travel difficult. The Incas responded with an extensive road network, known as the Qhapaq Ñan. Roads, bridges, stairways and relay stations connected administrative centres and allowed armies, officials and messengers to move across the empire.

The state organised labour through systems of reciprocal obligation. The mit'a required communities to provide labour for public projects, military service and other state needs. In return, the state was expected to organise resources and provide support during shortages and major ceremonies. These relationships were not equal or voluntary in the modern sense; they were part of an imperial system that demanded service and redistributed goods.

The empire was divided into administrative regions and local communities were organised through kinship-based units often called ayllu. Officials monitored populations and production. The quipu, a system of knotted cords, recorded numerical information and may have preserved other forms of data. Researchers continue to investigate how much information quipus could encode beyond quantities.

## Agriculture and engineering

Inca agriculture adapted to difficult environments. Terraces reduced erosion and created cultivable land on steep slopes. Irrigation channels moved water to fields, while storage facilities helped preserve food for periods of scarcity or military campaigns. Communities cultivated potatoes, maize, quinoa and other crops at different elevations. The empire's ecological range allowed it to draw on diverse agricultural zones.

Stone architecture is among the most celebrated achievements of the Inca. Builders fitted massive stones together with remarkable precision, often without mortar. Cusco's walls and the royal estate of Machu Picchu demonstrate sophisticated planning and construction. Machu Picchu was likely a royal estate or ceremonial centre associated with the fifteenth-century ruler Pachacuti, although aspects of its precise function remain debated.

## Religion and political authority

Inca religion recognised a range of deities and sacred forces. Inti, the Sun, was especially important to royal ideology, while Viracocha, Pachamama and other beings held significance in different traditions. Sacred places known as huacas could include mountains, springs, stones and ancestral sites. The ruler was linked to divine authority, and state ceremonies helped reinforce the relationship between political power, landscape and religion.

The empire incorporated local religious practices, but conquest could also involve the relocation of communities, the transfer of sacred objects and the imposition of state ceremonies. Such policies helped the Inca manage conquered populations while preserving the authority of local leaders who cooperated with imperial rule.

## Civil war and Spanish conquest

After Huayna Capac's death, a succession conflict developed between his sons Atahualpa and Huáscar. The civil war weakened the empire shortly before the arrival of Spanish forces led by Francisco Pizarro. In 1532, Pizarro captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca and later executed him. Spanish forces exploited internal divisions and formed alliances with Indigenous groups opposed to Inca rule.

The conquest was not completed in a single event. Inca resistance continued, and a Neo-Inca state survived at Vilcabamba until 1572. Disease, warfare, forced labour and colonial restructuring caused enormous disruption to Andean societies.

## Enduring legacy

The Inca Empire left lasting marks on language, agriculture, roads, architecture and political memory. Quechua remains widely spoken, and many Andean communities preserve agricultural and cultural practices with deep historical roots. The Qhapaq Ñan is recognised as a major heritage route, while Inca stonework continues to attract scholarly and public attention.

Understanding the Inca requires looking beyond spectacular monuments. The empire depended on the knowledge and labour of farmers, builders, herders, administrators and local communities across a vast landscape. Its history reveals a distinctive form of state organisation adapted to the environmental and social conditions of the Andes.

en.title: The Maya Civilization
en.place: Mesoamerica, including present-day southern Mexico and Central America
en.text:
## A civilization across Mesoamerica

The Maya civilization developed across a broad region that includes the Yucatan Peninsula, Guatemala, Belize and parts of Honduras and El Salvador. Maya history spans thousands of years, from early village communities to the rise of major cities and the continuation of Maya societies into the present. The Classic period, approximately 250–900 CE, saw the growth of powerful city-states, monumental architecture, sophisticated writing and mathematical and astronomical knowledge.

The Maya did not form a single unified empire. Their political landscape consisted of competing and allied kingdoms, each with its own ruler, court and territory. Cities such as Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, Copan and Caracol became important centres at different times. Warfare, marriage alliances, trade and diplomacy connected these polities.

## Cities, kings and monuments

Maya cities were organised around ceremonial centres containing temples, palaces, plazas, ballcourts and elite residences. Monumental buildings were often constructed in stages, with later rulers enlarging or covering earlier structures. Tall stepped pyramids and carved stone monuments communicated political authority and religious meaning.

Rulers were central to public ritual. Stelae and inscriptions recorded accessions, victories, dynastic events and ceremonies. Kings claimed relationships with ancestors and deities, presenting their authority as part of a cosmic order. Yet political power was never absolute: rival dynasties, noble families and regional communities shaped the fortunes of each kingdom.

Maya cities depended on surrounding agricultural landscapes. Farmers cultivated maize, beans, squash and other crops, using varied methods suited to local soils and rainfall. In some areas, raised fields, terraces, reservoirs and water-management systems supported dense populations. The tropical environment required detailed knowledge of seasons, forests and water.

## Writing, mathematics and astronomy

The Maya developed one of the most sophisticated writing systems in the ancient Americas. Their hieroglyphic script recorded names, dates, political events, rituals and historical narratives. It combined signs representing words and syllables. Decipherment advanced significantly during the twentieth century, allowing scholars to reconstruct royal histories from inscriptions on monuments, ceramics and manuscripts.

Maya mathematics included a vigesimal, or base-twenty, system and a symbol for zero. The use of zero enabled complex calculations and was part of a broader intellectual tradition. Maya astronomers observed the movements of the Sun, Moon, Venus and other celestial bodies. Calendrical systems organised ritual and political life, while Long Count dates recorded time across long cycles.

The Maya calendar was not a single simple device but a set of interlocking systems, including the 260-day ritual calendar and the 365-day solar calendar. Their combination created a Calendar Round cycle, while the Long Count provided a way to count longer spans of time. These systems helped organise ceremonies, agriculture and royal commemoration.

## Religion and the natural world

Maya religious traditions included many deities and supernatural beings associated with rain, maize, death, creation and celestial forces. The maize god was especially important in narratives of life, renewal and human origin. Sacred caves, mountains, springs and cenotes were understood as places of connection with powerful forces and the ancestors.

Ritual practices varied across time and region. Offerings, bloodletting, dance, feasting and ballgames could have religious and political significance. The ballgame was played in courts found at many Maya sites, although rules and meanings varied. It could represent mythological themes, political competition and community identity.

## Transformation of the Classic cities

Many southern lowland cities experienced political fragmentation and population decline between the eighth and tenth centuries. This process is often called the Classic Maya collapse, but it was not the disappearance of the Maya people. The causes differed by region and likely included warfare, dynastic instability, environmental stress, drought, soil pressures and changing trade networks.

Maya communities continued to thrive in the northern Yucatan and elsewhere. Postclassic centres such as Chichen Itza and Mayapan became influential. Spanish invasion in the sixteenth century brought warfare, disease, religious suppression and colonial rule, but Maya resistance continued for centuries. Some independent Maya states survived into the seventeenth century.

## Maya people today

Millions of Maya people live across Mexico and Central America today. They speak many Mayan languages and maintain diverse cultural, religious and community traditions. Contemporary Maya communities are not merely descendants of an ancient civilization; they are living peoples with modern political, intellectual and cultural lives.

The Maya legacy includes writing, mathematics, astronomy, architecture, agriculture and historical knowledge. It also reminds us that complex societies can be politically decentralised. Rather than a single empire, the Maya world was a changing network of cities and communities whose achievements developed over many centuries.
